# Pricing a Protected Draft Pick as a Financial Option, in Basketball Units

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster (with co-author Michael Bins, caption spelling) prices a draft pick plus its protection scheme (a "draft pick asset") in player-value terms, not money (SIn6IyYQEVI [00:31], [01:02], [03:05]). A protection is a condition that lets the trading team keep the pick if it lands in a protected range, with the pick rolling over to later years (the Lakers 2015 pick was top-5 protected in 2015, top-3 for a couple of years, then unprotected in 2018) (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:02] to [03:05]). The analogy is a financial option: the protection plays the part of the contract terms, and the volatility of the underlying value matters (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40], [08:10]). He does not use the option math directly, only its principles (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:10], [08:40]). Three steps (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]):
1. **Characterize volatility of the underlying asset.** Module one: an Elo-rating season simulation that gives a distribution of finishing position (1 means worst, to match how picks are dealt), run 10,000 times over the roughly 20 remaining games at the trade deadline (SIn6IyYQEVI [09:10], [09:40]). Module two: cumulative distributions of player value by pick position, using Basketball-Reference history for first-round picks, with win shares as the metric (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [10:42]).
2. **Assess the contract conditions.** A 10,000-run Monte Carlo combines lottery probabilities and the protection scheme into a distribution of win shares summed over a player's first five years (SIn6IyYQEVI [11:14], [11:45]).
3. **Account for market risk** with a Wang transform (see [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]]), reducing the distribution to a single price (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:16], [13:17]).
He states the purpose is to help a team decide where to place protections when trading a pick away or trading for one (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:09]). Because millions of protection schemes exist, one base pick can have millions of trade values (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). The model is modular, so the player value metric can be swapped (SIn6IyYQEVI [10:11], [19:23]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is the option parallel: how likely the pick is to fall inside versus outside the protected range drives value (SIn6IyYQEVI [07:40]). He gives no tested argument that this transfer from finance is accurate; he says they adapt the principles "with our own methods" (SIn6IyYQEVI [08:40]).

**When to apply** — As a template for any asset that arrives as an uncertain outcome with contract conditions: model the uncertainty source, apply the conditions in simulation, then price. Inference: for Baylor, the closest analogs are recruiting and portal classes (an uncertain future player value) rather than any monitoring work; the applications note flags low direct use for Applied Performance. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: one worked example (see [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]]), calibration from few pick-for-pick trades, and no outcome test. Limits the speaker names: the season simulation does not account for player movement, the work was done on personal computers with limited time, and time discounting and the option value of rolling a pick over are not explicitly modeled (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48], [19:23], [22:26]). College rosters have no barter market with protections, so the option analogy may not carry over; the outcome data are NBA win shares for first-round picks only.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the Lakers 2015 first-round pick that went from the Suns to the Sixers at the 2015 deadline, priced with and without its top-5 protection (SIn6IyYQEVI [02:33], [12:46]).

**Related** — [[principle--value-an-uncertain-asset-by-its-outcome-distribution-not-its-mean]]; [[claim--traded-pick-protections-cluster-at-top-5-10-and-14]]; [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]].

# Validating a Causal Metric When the True Effect Cannot Be Observed

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins notes that with observational data "we don't have the underlying causal effect" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10], [08:40]), so he checks the metric indirectly (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09] to [09:10]):
1. **Face validity against honors:** top-10 rankings by position (defensive end, defensive tackle, outside and inside linebacker), with All-Pro and Pro Bowl players marked; he reports a "much better correlation" than supervised models (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09], [07:39]).
2. **Team-level aggregation:** mean individual EPS plotted against mean individual EPA for tacklers shows a strong negative correlation, which he says helps explain 41% of the variance in tackle play outcomes (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).
3. **Synthetic data:** against independent models, his model has "significantly higher R-squared" and "much lower RMSE"; no values are given (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).
4. **Salary rank:** better ranking of non-rookie players by salary and by Pro Bowl status (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is that individual causal estimates that aggregate to team results and match honors are capturing "genuine defensive value, not just the statistical artifacts" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]). The talk does not say why salary and honors should be unbiased proxies. Inference: honors and salaries are themselves partly produced by tackle counts, the quantity he criticizes, so agreement with them is weak evidence.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a model with no ground truth: ask what the synthetic-data test knew that the model did not, what outside labels were used, and whether those labels share the model's bias. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" for individualized thresholds (Explicit). Inference: that is a within-athlete noise check; the checks above are between-player, a different question.

**When NOT to apply** — Only the 41% and 68% figures are given as numbers. R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons are stated as better with no values (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]). `untested`. Validation is by synthetic data and honors, not by a known true effect, and the speaker's claims of being first and of better ranking are his own in a competition presentation. Not a recipe for non-NFL data.

**Example** — The speaker's: the team-level plot, where better-tackler teams (higher mean EPS) tend to allow better outcomes, 41% of variance (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], [[heuristic--year-to-year-stability-as-test-of-real-skill]], a different validity check on the ESPN receiver metric.

# Credit the Gap Between Expected and Observed Yards to the Passer, and Read Agreement With Care

**What it is** — Burke's second variant estimates expected yards two ways: for the play configuration as a whole, or assuming each receiver is the target. Comparing what happened with the estimate, "we can credit that amount above or below expected to the quarterback's performance" (EeBgUCYhezc [12:23]). Example: Jared Goff (caption spelling "Jared Goff") was expected at 7.8 yards per attempt in 2018, actually had 9.9 on targeted passes, a difference of +2.1, credited to him (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]). The 2018 top five and bottom five passers on this measure are shown on his chart (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]).

He plots that residual against how often the passer agreed with the model's recommended target. Rookies sit low on production against expectation and high on agreement, which he reads as "the safe thing" and as the binding constraint on their offense (EeBgUCYhezc [13:33], [14:05]). The most aggressive passers sit on the left (EeBgUCYhezc [14:05]). He expected a positive correlation between agreement and production and found "slightly negative", which he explains as "a severe selection bias" (EeBgUCYhezc [14:38]). His reasoning: you cannot ask any quarterback to do what Aaron Rodgers would do, because he "may not have the physical attributes". The talk does not test this explanation.

**Why it works** — The speaker's logic is that the model holds the situation fixed, so whatever differs from expected belongs to the passer. He also says the credit is isolated "to a very large extent" from teammates but not from receivers or scheme (EeBgUCYhezc [20:52]). Inference: this is a residual method, and the residual absorbs everything the model leaves out (hands, height, vertical position, scheme, as he lists them at [22:01]).

**When to apply** — As a template for "expected versus observed" where a model can state what a typical athlete would produce in this situation. Inference: the same shape fits GPS (expected drill load versus observed). Always report what the residual cannot isolate.

Eric's baseline: "I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q12, about ACWR.) Inference: that skepticism toward a single ratio read without context applies equally to a residual credited to one person.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not read agreement with the model as decision quality: the talk's own data show it did not track production, and the explanation is unverified. The talk is single-season (2018 through week 12) NFL data and a "proof of concept" (EeBgUCYhezc [23:32]). Do not use a residual to rank individuals when the model lacks inputs that differ by individual. Marked untested because the speaker shows no validation of the credit, only the chart and one worked example.

**Contested:** [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25, Ben Jenkins) argues that residuals from a prediction model rely on correlation and are not a causal estimate of player impact, which is the approach used here. The two talks use the data differently; this entry's method is a residual in exactly the sense that talk criticizes.

**Example** — Goff: 7.8 expected, 9.9 observed, +2.1 (EeBgUCYhezc [12:54]).

**Related** — [[claim--deepqb-target-accuracy-60-percent-against-20-percent-chance]]; [[framework--deepqb-receiver-target-model-inputs-and-four-variants]].

# Name a Metric for What It Literally Measures and Scale It for Its Audience

**What it is** — Two choices the panel describes for public metrics.
- **Name:** for the pass-block and pass-rush "win rate," they avoided calling it a rating or grade, to avoid implying it is "the end-all be-all" on how good a lineman or rusher is. It is the percent of the time a player sustains or beats a block for 2.5 seconds, with no other implication, like a batting average (teg9SfzpMy0 [41:11], [41:43], [42:14]).
- **Scale:** for fans, "z-scores" were not digestible, so the receiver score became 0 to 99, like QBR; a panelist adds that for a team they would build a more sophisticated final number or set of units (teg9SfzpMy0 [42:14], [42:44]).

**Why it works** — The panel's reasoning is audience fit: fans are "kind of checked out" by z-scores, and a name implying a verdict claims more than the number delivers (teg9SfzpMy0 [41:43], [42:14]). They give no test of the choice. Inference: a plain-language definition lets a reader see what the number can and cannot say.

**When to apply** — Whenever a number goes to coaches or athletes. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): coach-facing reports are built by strength staff for most teams, and sport science staff provide them when applicable (Explicit). Inference: the person building the report picks the label, so name the number for what it counts ("percent of reps above a speed threshold"), not as a grade.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication practice from a media organization whose stated aim is to "engage and entertain the fans," not to help a team win (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]). `untested`. The panel says a team version would differ (teg9SfzpMy0 [42:44]). A bounded 0 to 99 scale clips extreme values (teg9SfzpMy0 [43:15]). Fan-friendly scaling hides units that a performance staff would need for decisions.

**Example** — The panel's: "win rate," given a plain definition instead of a grade-like name (teg9SfzpMy0 [41:43]).

**Related** — [[framework--weight-mixed-unit-components-by-correlation-with-an-outcome]], [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]], a library framework on keeping the measurement separate from its interpretation.

# If a Coach Ignores the Report, Change the Question, Then Show Athletes Their Own Data

**What it is** — Three episodes from Morris's talk:
- **The trashed report.** He put a report he was "really proud of" on the offensive-line coach's desk and the coach threw it in the trash (QLdbKUiNadg [04:04]). His first reaction was that he had a PhD and was the expert; he then concluded that his data "was not having the right conversation" (QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]).
- **The reframe.** The coach later asked "how much they're bangin in practice" (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]). Morris answered by first measuring the game (about 45 contacts, load per contact about 2.22) so the practice figures were comparable (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13], [07:45]).
- **Athlete buy-in.** Athletes must be "connected" to their data internally and externally, "because if you don't they don't have a lot of buy-in they feel like lab rats" (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]). He mentions an earlier case, the Eagles under Chip Kelly, where players pushed back on more intense work (QLdbKUiNadg [17:38]).
He also notes that coaches grade in subjective terms, and without objective data a dispute is "just your opinion versus my opinion" (QLdbKUiNadg [01:02], [01:32]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that the report answered a question the coach was not asking. He gives no evidence beyond his own experience. Inference: a coach's own question (here, contact in practice versus game) gets attention, while a generic report does not.

**When to apply** — When a coach does not read or use a report. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." Inference: the coach's question is the "where to look", and the data answer it. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams." Inference: at Baylor the person who reframes the report for the coach is often the strength staff member.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: anecdote, a single coach, a single athlete group. The talk does not report whether the reframed reports changed decisions or results. It does not support using data to win arguments with a coach; the speaker describes the reverse (first reaction: "you should listen to me", QLdbKUiNadg [04:34]). The Eagles reference is a second-hand recollection by the speaker.

**Example** — The talk's own: the practice-versus-game contact comparison was built because the line coach wanted to see "how much they're bangin" (QLdbKUiNadg [07:13]).

# The No-Tanking Condition: Winning Must Pay at Least as Much as Losing

**What it is** — In Evan Monroe's model teams care about two prizes, making the playoffs and getting the first pick, each at a fixed value (-6pe_zOKCig [09:46]). A team chooses to try to win or try to lose by a "no tanking condition": the benefit from winning a game must be at least the benefit from losing it (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). Winning raises or leaves unchanged the chance of the playoffs, but under the current system lowers the draft chance; losing does the reverse (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). The speaker says the condition fails in many scenarios under the current system, with a simple case: a fixed lottery that favors the worst records, applied to a team already eliminated (-6pe_zOKCig [10:49], [11:20]). His design target is that the condition holds in every game (-6pe_zOKCig [21:03]).

**Why it works** — Stated by the speaker as "very intuitive"; the logic is the one-line comparison above (-6pe_zOKCig [10:17]). He gives no further mechanism.

**When to apply** — As a one-question audit of any measure that feeds a consequence: could a participant gain by scoring worse? Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were abandoned after about a year because the consistent, low-effort answers they rewarded carried no signal, and mRSI from force-plate jumps replaced them as the daily readiness marker as "objective, consistent, and actionable" (Explicit, SportSmith, 2026-02-19). Inference: ask the no-tanking question of each daily number that changes load or playing time (for example, whether a low score lowers practice load, giving an athlete a reason to hold back on a jump). The talk does not claim objective measures are immune, and says nothing about athlete testing; the link is analogy only.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a model condition, not an empirical finding about teams or athletes. It needs a decision that actually follows from the number and that the participant can see; if the result drives no consequence the athlete cares about, the concern is moot. The two-prize model, rational-actor assumption and fixed prize values are the speaker's simplifications. Do not import the lottery math; a handful of athletes cannot reveal incentives.

**Example** — The speaker's own: an eliminated team facing a fixed, bad-team-favoring lottery should try to lose every game that affects its ranking (-6pe_zOKCig [11:20]).

**Related** — [[claim--lottery-on-final-ranking-alone-cannot-favor-worst-team-without-tank-incentive]]; [[framework--time-dependent-lottery-with-dynamically-frozen-odds]].

============================== principle--value-an-uncertain-asset-by-its-outcome-distribution-not-its-mean.md

# Value an Uncertain Asset by Its Whole Outcome Distribution, Not Its Mean

**What it is** — Benjamin Foster shows that two assets with different tails can have similar averages. A base draft pick "looks like a distribution of possible pick position outcomes," so trading it gives the other team that set of outcomes (SIn6IyYQEVI [03:36]). A protection changes the distribution, not just its center (SIn6IyYQEVI [04:07]). Taking the mean "doesn't account for the variance," and the extreme outcomes (picks one through three, the chance of getting LeBron James or "someone who might change your franchise's history") are exactly what protection removes, so the model weights them (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [13:17]). In the unprotected case the priced value sits far to the right of the mean because of the tail; in the protected case the price is "relatively close to the expected value" (SIn6IyYQEVI [15:49]). The tool is a risk adjustment (the Wang transform) with a market price of risk (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [13:47]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that teams care about outcomes in the tails, and the market prices that preference (SIn6IyYQEVI [13:17], [14:18]). He gives no empirical test that the adjustment is correct.

**When to apply** — When comparing options with different spreads (a high-ceiling prospect versus a safe contributor): show the range of outcomes in one unit, then say which end the decision values. Inference: a recruiting board could express each prospect as best, typical and worst case in one unit and compare classes by spread, as the applications note proposes. Eric's baseline: no direct link found.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the speaker presents a method and one worked example with no validation, and the risk parameter is calibrated on few pick-for-pick trades (SIn6IyYQEVI [14:48]). If decision makers value only the average, or the outcome data are too thin to build a distribution (small samples at one position), a distribution adds false precision. The adjustment depends on the assumed market risk preference, which is a stated assumption, not a measurement.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the protected and unprotected versions of the same pick (SIn6IyYQEVI [12:46], [15:49]); the numbers are in [[case-study--lakers-2015-pick-protections-removed-about-half-its-value]].

**Related** — [[framework--price-a-protected-draft-pick-like-a-financial-option]]; [[heuristic--market-risk-preference-differs-by-pick-position-in-the-draft-pick-model]].
